steps.body: Every number can **explode into its worth-pieces**: 452 = 400 + 50 + 2. That's called expanded form. Building goes the other way — snap the pieces back together. Nothing is ever lost in either direction; it's the same number, unpacked or packed.
Explode a number yourself — every piece carries its spot's worth.

widget.prompt: Break 375 into its worth-pieces. Build the expanded form, biggest piece first.

commonBuilds.feedback: The 7 parks in the TENS spot of 375 — its piece is worth 70, not 7. Worth-pieces carry their spot.
30 would come from a 3 in the tens spot — but 375's tens digit is 7. Its middle piece is 70.

widget.missFeedback: Read the spots of 375: 3 hundreds (300), 7 tens (70), 5 ones (5) — joined with +.

predict.prompt: In 375's expanded form, the middle digit 7 shows up as…
predict.reveal: The 7 sits in the tens spot, so its worth-piece is 70: 375 = 300 + 70 + 5. Writing + 7 instead would shortchange the number by 63 — expanded form pays each digit its full place value.

steps.body: Empty spots leave no piece behind.
explanationVariants: 608 has 6 hundreds, 0 tens, 8 ones — the zero's piece is nothing, so only 600 + 8 remain.
The placeholder 0 holds a spot inside the number, but in pieces it simply vanishes: no tens piece exists.

options.feedback: 6 hundreds and 8 ones; the empty tens spot contributes no piece at all.
That reads the 6 as tens — but in 608 the 6 parks in the hundreds. Its piece is 600.
The 8 sits in the ONES spot — the zero holds the tens. There's no 80 hiding in 608.
Those are the bare digits with their worth stripped off. Pieces keep their spots: the 6 is worth 600.

steps.body: Why explode numbers at all? **Pieces let you work on one spot at a time.** For 452 + 30, only the tens piece changes: 50 + 30 = 80, so the answer is 400 + 80 + 2 = 482. The hundreds and ones never even wake up.

explanationVariants: Stack the pieces: five hundreds, four tens, three ones snap into 543.

commonErrors.feedback: 12 added the bare digits (5 + 4 + 3), throwing the worth away. The pieces are 500, 40, and 3 — whole values.
5403 glued the pieces' digits side by side. Snapping means each piece fills its own SPOT: 5 in hundreds, 4 in tens, 3 in ones.
534 swapped the tens and ones — the 40 piece fills the tens spot (4), the 3 piece fills the ones.

widget.fallbackFeedback: One piece per spot: hundreds from the 500, tens from the 40, ones from the 3.

steps.body: Zeros make near-twin numbers — pieces tell them apart.

widget.prompt: Match each number to its worth-pieces. Watch where the zeros sit!

pairErrors.feedback: 200 + 90 has nine TENS — that's 290. In 209 the zero holds the tens spot, so its 9 is just nine ones.

widget.missFeedback: Explode each one: which spot does its zero hold, and which spots have real pieces?
widget.successFeedback: 290, 209, 920 — same digits, different spots, three different numbers. Pieces never lie.

steps.body: Use pieces to add without a pencil.
explanationVariants: Only the tens piece changes: 452 is 400 + 50 + 2, and 50 + 30 = 80, so 400 + 80 + 2 = 482.
Adding 30 is adding 3 tens — the tens digit climbs from 5 to 8 while the others sleep.

commonErrors.feedback: 455 added 3 ONES. But 30 is 3 tens — it belongs to the middle piece: 50 + 30.
752 added 3 HUNDREDS. The 30 piece is tens-sized — only the tens spot should move.
485 moved the tens AND the ones. Adding 30 touches exactly one piece: the 50 becomes 80, and the 2 stays put.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Pieces: 400 + 50 + 2. The +30 joins the tens piece only.

hints: 679. Now find its tens digit (7) and ones digit (9).
Swap those two digits — the hundreds digit never moves.
explanationVariants: Snap: 679. Swap tens and ones: the 7 and 9 trade spots → 697.
After the swap the pieces read 600 + 90 + 7, which snaps into 697.

widget.prompt: A number explodes into 600 + 70 + 9. Swap its tens digit with its ones digit, then snap it back together. What number do you get?

commonErrors.feedback: 679 is the number BEFORE the swap — the snap worked! Now trade the tens digit (7) with the ones digit (9).
976 moved the 9 all the way to the hundreds. Only the tens and ones trade places; the 6 stays home.
769 swapped the hundreds with the tens. The swap is between the LAST two spots: 7 and 9.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Snap first (679), then trade just the last two digits.

steps.body: Numbers come apart in your hands now.
takeaways: Expanded form: each digit becomes a piece worth its spot.
Empty spots leave no piece — but inside the number, their zero still holds the place.
Pieces let you change one spot at a time — mental math's favorite trick.
steps.teaser: which number is bigger? The spots settle every argument in one glance.

concept.body: Quick rewind. To explode a number, give **each digit its spot's worth**: in 46, the 4 is in tens (piece: 40) and the 6 is in ones (piece: 6). So 46 = 40 + 6. To snap back, drop each piece into its spot.

explanationVariants: 83's 8 parks in tens: piece 80. The 3 is three ones: 80 + 3.
Say it out loud — eighty-three — and the pieces name themselves.

options.feedback: Eight tens and three ones — the pieces of 83.
Those are bare digits — the 8's spot makes it worth 80. Pieces keep their worth.
800 needs a hundreds spot, but 83 has only two spots. The 8 is eight TENS: 80.
